A shared rainwater system at Port Stewart

A proposed shared rainwater-harvesting system giving the Lama Lama community safe drinking water through both the wet and dry seasons.

Design Area(s): 6. Water Resilience   Design Opportunity: 6.2 Drinking Water Quality and Treatment

Keywords: rainwater harvesting, drinking water quality, Lama Lama, Port Stewart, Cape York, slow-sand filtration, solar UV

Proposal Summary

The project aims to address unsafe and unreliable drinking water at Port Stewart through shared rainwater systems, each serving a cluster of about five nearby homes. Rain from household roofs is cleaned, stored in two shared tanks, filtered and treated with solar-powered ultraviolet light, then delivered by gravity to one shared outlet. This is a student proposal and has not been approved by the community or the Yintjingga Aboriginal Corporation (YAC).

Overview of Design

  • The system collects wet-season rain and stores it for the dry season, so the community does not depend on the Stewart River.
  • Implementation is supported by staged construction, supplier training and Ranger-led maintenance.
  • Components: roof gutters and downpipes, first-flush diverters, two 10,000 L tanks on a raised mound, a slow-sand filter, a solar-powered UV unit with battery, and a shared outlet.
  • Residents of each cluster of about five homes would collect treated water from that cluster’s shared outlet.

Key Considerations

  • It adds to existing sources (the Ranger Base and carted water) and is not a full replacement in long dry periods.
  • Maintenance uses skills Rangers already have, and old batteries must leave on the supply truck.
  • Water quality has not yet been tested. Laboratory testing is required before anyone drinks from the system.
  • Next step: consult YAC and the Lama Lama community before any detailed design. Costs still need supplier confirmation.

Proposed Materials and Cost Summary

  • Purchased materials: tanks, gutters and diverters, slow-sand filter, solar UV unit and battery, pipes and fittings.
  • Estimated cost (AUD) for one cluster: about $30,400 one-off plus about $2,200 a year for maintenance. Approximate, to be confirmed with suppliers.

Port Stewart’s river floods in the wet, dries up in the dry, and carries metals the community has good reason not to trust. This design never touches the river.

Project context

Port Stewart is a Lama Lama community on Cape York, Queensland. The Yintjingga Aboriginal Corporation (YAC), led by Lama Lama Traditional Owners, is the community partner (Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations, n.d.; North Australian Indigenous Land and Sea Management Alliance, n.d.). The project responds to the 2026 EWB Challenge brief, Design Area 6 (Water Resilience) and Design Opportunity 6.2 (Drinking Water Quality and Treatment) (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a). Through co-design workshops, Lama Lama Elders, EWB and the Centre for Appropriate Technology agreed that rainwater harvesting should be the path forward (Low, 2025). The Stewart River has been the main source, but its flow swings between flood and almost nothing and it carries arsenic and manganese (Queensland Department of Environment and Science, 2021).

01

Seasonal extremes

The river floods in the wet season and the water source dries up in the dry. (Water Source, 2018)

02

Metals in the river

Testing detected arsenic and manganese at the Stewart River site. (Queensland Department of Environment and Science, 2021)

03

A fix that stalled

A bore intake design from 2020–21 was never built because construction funding wasn’t secured. (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2021)

04

Trust has gone

Most residents have stopped using the river supply. (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a)

What has been tried

Figure 6. Timeline of water supply attempts at Port Stewart. Select a year to read more.

Existing solutions elsewhere

Think Water. A national franchise that supplies pumps, filtration (including UV) and rainwater tanks to homes, farms and businesses (Irrigation Australia, n.d.-a; n.d.-b).

Kadjina community upgrades. Filtration that removes iron and manganese, with automatic disinfection, in a government-backed $1.9M project (Morse, 2026; Water Corporation, 2026).

Why this is not enough

A cyclone destroyed the original supply in 2006 (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2019), a 2020 to 2021 bore intake was never built because funding was not secured (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2021), and the 2024 Ranger Base rainwater system, funded by a $40,000 Yaru Foundation donation, does not serve the homes (Prestipino, 2024; Yaru Water, 2024; Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a). A rainwater system commissioned at Port Stewart in August 2025 delivers water that meets the Australian Drinking Water Guidelines, but house connections are still to come (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026b). River water is still unsafe and most residents have stopped using it (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a).

Problem description

The Lama Lama community needs safe, reliable drinking water that is available year-round and easy to maintain locally.

Poor water quality, seasonal extremes and limited infrastructure prevent this (Water Source, 2018; Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a; Yaru Water, 2024). The ideal is a supply that avoids the river’s metals, does not depend on transported water, works in both seasons with minimal maintenance, and is developed with the community and Rangers (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2021; Yaru Water, 2024).

What the project aims to achieve

The project aims to design a shared rainwater system for each cluster of about five homes that removes dependence on the river, can be built in stages, needs minimal power and chemicals, and can be looked after with local skills, supporting YAC’s priorities of return to Country and caring for Country (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a).

Why rainwater and not the alternatives

Design criteria

Seven criteria were used to judge the options. Each comes from the design brief and the project’s sources, and each is tied to what the community needs.

Table 3. Design criteria, what each means and why it matters.
CriterionWhat it meansWhy it matters
Safe waterMeets the Australian Drinking Water Guidelines and avoids the river’s metals.The river has shown arsenic and manganese, and most residents no longer trust it (Queensland Department of Environment and Science, 2021; Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a).
Seasonal reliabilityWater is available in both the wet and dry seasons.The river floods then dries up, and the dry-season population nearly doubles (Water Source, 2018; Prestipino, 2024).
Cyclone resilienceWithstands cyclone conditions and can be shut down beforehand.A cyclone destroyed the original supply in 2006 (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2019).
Low maintenanceNeeds minimal power and chemicals and can be looked after with local skills.The community can be cut off for months, and Rangers already maintain solar systems (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a).
Builds on existingAdds to existing infrastructure instead of starting again.This keeps cost down and fits what is already funded (Yaru Water, 2024).
Fundable in stagesCan be paid for and delivered in affordable steps.The 2020 to 2021 design was never built because its funding was needed all at once (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2021).
Community ledDeveloped with and owned by the community and Rangers.Local training supports long-term maintenance (Prestipino, 2024).

The team looked at four ways to give Port Stewart safe water. Each is scored against the design criteria in the decision matrix below.

01 / 04

Repair the existing river filter

It already failed once and keeps breaking down during the dry season, and most residents have stopped trusting and using this water. (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a)

02 / 04

Bore intake with aeration

The 2020 Arup and EWB design. It works at nearby Wujal Wujal, but needed a large amount of construction funding all at once, which is why it was never built. (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2021)

03 / 04

Chemical treatment

Chlorination needs regular chemical deliveries into a community that is cut off for months each wet season. (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a)

04 / 04

Cluster rainwater harvesting

Proposed solution

Avoids the river entirely, can be built in stages, needs no chemicals and uses proven technology. (Kalt et al., 2014; PV Magazine Australia, 2020)

Decision matrix

Each option is rated from 1 to 5 against the criteria in Table 3 (1 = does not meet, 2 = meets poorly, 3 = meets partly, 4 = meets mostly, 5 = meets fully). Each criterion also has a weight from 1 to 5, set to 1 until the team agrees different weights. The weighted total is the sum of weight multiplied by score.

Table 4. Decision matrix with scores from 1 to 5 and equal weights.

Selected solution: cluster rainwater harvesting, with one shared system for each cluster of about five homes. With these scores and equal weights it scores 26 of 35, ahead of the 2020 bore intake (19), repairing the existing filter (16) and chemical treatment (14).

Is the water safe to drink?

Safe by design, not yet proven by testing. Each step below is backed by published guidance or research, but the team has not built the system or tested water from it. Untreated roof rainwater can carry bacterial and protozoan pathogens (Ahmed et al., 2011), so every step matters, and the system must be commissioned and tested before anyone drinks from it.

What it deals with

Dust, leaves and bird droppings washed off roofs.

What the research says

First-flush diverters are recommended in Australian guidance (enHealth, 2010), and Queensland requires at least 20 L discarded and devices checked every six months (Queensland Government, 2009).

What it does not do

Does not remove germs already in the tank, and a blocked diverter stops working.

What it deals with

Animals, insects and mosquitoes entering the tanks.

What the research says

Queensland rules require mosquito-proof screens or flap valves on every tank opening (Queensland Government, 2009).

What it does not do

Does not stop sediment building up, so tanks still need cleaning.

What it deals with

Bacteria, protozoa, some viruses and cloudiness.

What the research says

Studies report 2 to 3 log removal of E. coli, 1.5 to 2 log of viruses and over 5 log of Cryptosporidium (Hijnen et al., 2004).

What it does not do

Needs a ripening period, works best at a steady flow and with clear water, and only partly removes arsenic (National Drinking Water Clearinghouse, 2000).

What it deals with

Bacteria, viruses and protozoa that pass the filter, with no chemicals.

What the research says

UV readily inactivates bacteria and protozoa, and viruses are the most resistant (Hijnen et al., 2006), so it follows the filter. A solar UVA unit reached a 4-log E. coli reduction in a different design (Kalt et al., 2014).

What it does not do

Leaves no lasting disinfectant, needs power and clear water, and needs the supplier’s proof of its dose.

What it deals with

Whether the other barriers are working.

What the research says

No E. coli should be detected in any 100 mL sample, and detection needs immediate action (National Health and Medical Research Council, n.d.). Rainwater needs “low maintenance, not no maintenance” (SA Health, n.d.).

What it does not do

Not done yet. The team has not tested water from this system, and testing is required before anyone drinks from it.

Proposed testing plan (for discussion)
  • Pilot test. Run a small pilot filter first, because slow-sand filter performance cannot be predicted from the raw water alone (National Drinking Water Clearinghouse, 2000).
  • Before first use. Run the filter to waste until it is mature. Have a laboratory test water from the commissioned system for E. coli, turbidity, pH and the chemical risks from roofs and pipes. Ask the UV supplier for evidence of the dose their unit delivers.
  • Routine checks. Trained Rangers check the UV indicator and battery, look at the water, and inspect the first-flush device and screens at least every six months and after big storms, noting each check in a logbook.
  • Regular water tests. E. coli tests at the tap on a schedule agreed with Queensland Health, with occasional laboratory samples.
  • If a test fails. Stop drinking from the outlet, use the Ranger Base or carted water, find the cause, fix it and re-test before restarting.
  • Safeguard to specify. A UV unit with an alarm and automatic shut-off so untreated water cannot flow if the lamp or power fails.

Proposal only. Not yet agreed with Queensland Health, the Yintjingga Aboriginal Corporation or a supplier.

The prototype: modelled, not yet tested

The prototype is a design model: the conceptual layout in Figure 10 and the sizing calculation below, using team assumptions from Week 10. The team has not built it or tested water from it. Change any input to see what it does.

What was modelled, and how

The team modelled how the parts fit together for one cluster of five homes (Figure 10) and whether the roofs and tanks are the right size (the calculator and Figure 11), because arrangement and sizing carry the biggest design risks. Figure 10 is an AI-generated concept illustration with numbered markers. The calculator runs a month-by-month water balance using the Bureau of Meteorology’s rainfall for Coen, about 60 km away (Bureau of Meteorology, n.d.-a; n.d.-b), and team assumptions for one cluster of about five homes, 20 people, 80 m² of roof per home, a runoff coefficient of 0.8 and 50 L per person per day.

litres collected in an average year

of yearly demand met from the tanks

What the model shows

Coen’s mean rainfall is about 1,200 mm a year, so the roofs could collect about 384,000 L in an average year against about 365,000 L of demand, a margin of only 5%. Two 10,000 L tanks fill in the wet season and run empty from about May until December. They would meet about 53% of demand (about 195,000 L), leaving about 170,000 L for the Ranger Base and carted water. Meeting all demand would need about 190,000 L of storage, which supports building in stages.

What published evidence shows

Table 8. Published evidence for each step. Each step works under the conditions studied; only testing can show that this system delivers safe water.
StepWhat the evidence reportsSource
Port Stewart systemA rainwater system commissioned at Port Stewart in August 2025 delivers water that complies with the Australian Drinking Water Guidelines. House connections are still to come.(Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026b)
Rainwater needs treatmentUntreated roof rainwater has carried bacterial and protozoan pathogens in household and communal tanks.(Ahmed et al., 2011)
Rainwater and healthA cohort study of 1,016 South Australian children found no higher gastroenteritis risk from untreated tank rainwater than from mains water (odds ratio 0.84).(Heyworth et al., 2006)
Field performance of sand filtersField studies report a median 80% E. coli reduction, only 17% of filters under 10 CFU per 100 mL, recontamination in storage, and 23% of households stopping use within a year.(Fiore et al., 2010)
Slow-sand filterStudies report 2 to 3 log removal of E. coli and coliforms, 1.5 to 2 log of viruses and over 5 log of Cryptosporidium.(Hijnen et al., 2004)
Filter and metalsTypical removal of over 95% of zinc, copper, cadmium and lead, over 67% of iron and manganese, but under 47% of arsenic.(National Drinking Water Clearinghouse, 2000)
UV disinfectionBacteria and protozoa are readily inactivated and viruses are the most UV-resistant, so UV after the filter covers weaker virus removal.(Hijnen et al., 2006)
Solar UV, remote rainwaterA solar UVA unit achieved a 4-log E. coli reduction (a different design).(Kalt et al., 2014)
Clear water for UVWater should be clear, ideally under 1 NTU, and UV units should alarm or shut off at low UV.(National Health and Medical Research Council, n.d.; NSW Health, n.d.)
RainfallCoen’s mean is about 1,184 to 1,201 mm a year, with about 92% from December to April.(Bureau of Meteorology, n.d.-a; n.d.-b)

Changes made and next tests

The rainfall assumption was lowered to about 1,200 mm. The filter evidence suggests one design change to test: slow-sand filters work best at a steady flow, so the filter should run slowly and continuously into a small treated-water tank feeding the UV unit and outlet (National Drinking Water Clearinghouse, 2000). Field studies also show filters underperforming and water being recontaminated in storage (Fiore et al., 2010), so UV, outlet hygiene and Ranger training matter. Next tests are a pilot slow-sand filter through the wet and dry seasons, laboratory tests of the commissioned system, and a check against Port Stewart rainfall records.

How it is built, run and paid for

  1. Select a central location close to the household cluster.
  2. Install or connect roof catchment, gutters and downpipes on nearby houses.
  3. Add first-flush diverters.
  4. Build a raised, secure base for flood and cyclone conditions.
  5. Install two 10,000 L shared tanks.
  6. Connect the slow-sand filter and the solar-powered UV unit.
  7. Test water quality and train local Rangers and community members in operation and maintenance.

Looking after it

Rangers already maintain solar systems at Port Stewart and Silver Plains. Training is given by the supplier at installation and passed on through the Junior Ranger program. A visual guide on site shows how to check the battery, clean the filter, replace parts and shut down before a cyclone. (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a)

Batteries are replaced every 5 to 10 years and leave on the same truck that brings supplies, because Port Stewart has no recycling service.

Evaluation

Success is judged by water test results, residents’ use of the outlet, and performance through the first wet and dry seasons, with a review after a year.

Ownership

Community members join construction, the supplier trains Rangers at installation, the Junior Ranger program passes knowledge on, and a visual guide stays on site (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a). Locals are already being trained in testing and maintenance for the Ranger Base system (Prestipino, 2024).

Effect on the future

A reliable supply near the homes supports return to Country and caring for Country and reduces reliance on the river and carted water (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a). It adds a maintenance task that needs a named person and a small budget.

Repairs

If something fails, Rangers follow the on-site guide to shut down safely and use the Ranger Base or carted water. Spare parts and old batteries travel on the supply truck (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a). The spares arrangement is yet to be agreed with a supplier.

Estimated costs (AUD)

Table 9. Estimated costs in Australian dollars.

Approximate estimates from the Week 10 presentation. Costs are for one cluster of about five homes. Catalogue prices were checked in October 2026 (see References), and the other lines are team estimates to be confirmed with suppliers. The Week 10 total of $35,700 was the one-off cost plus one year of maintenance; the tank line has since been revised from $8,000 to $4,900 using catalogue prices. Not yet costed: laboratory tests and field kits, UV lamp replacement, transport of samples, and end-of-life removal.

End of life

Batteries are replaced every 5 to 10 years and leave on the supply truck (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a). Removal of the tanks, filter housing and sand at end of life is not yet costed.

Funding

The Yaru Foundation’s $40,000 donation paid for the Ranger Base system, which shows donors can fund materials here (Prestipino, 2024; Yaru Water, 2024). The National Water Grid Fund has earmarked $150 million for remote and regional First Nations communities (Prestipino, 2024). EWB and corporate sponsors are other options, and eligibility has not been checked.

What this does not solve, and what comes next

The system adds to existing water sources. It is not a full replacement during long dry periods, and water comes from one shared outlet rather than a tap in every house. (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a)

Social, cultural, environmental and budgetary considerations

Social. A single outlet means residents still carry water, so hygiene matters because UV leaves no lasting protection. Trust has been lost (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a) and must be rebuilt through community-led testing.

Cultural. The river and sea are part of Lama Lama Country, and YAC’s priorities include caring for them (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2026a). The design avoids the river. The tank site should be chosen with YAC, and ground works may trigger Queensland cultural heritage obligations the team has not yet checked.

Environmental. Collecting rain from existing roofs avoids drawing more from the river, and solar power avoids the diesel pump (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2019). Impacts to manage are discarded first-flush water, the mound’s footprint and old batteries.

Budgetary. The one-off cost is about $30,400 plus about $2,200 a year, before testing and end-of-life costs. Staging avoids needing all the funding at once (Engineers Without Borders Australia, 2021).

Recommendations

  • Consult YAC and the Lama Lama community on this cluster design, building on EWB’s co-design workshops and aligning the testing plan with the program EWB is co-designing (Low, 2025).
  • Commission the system and test the water in a laboratory before first use, then agree a testing schedule with Queensland Health.
  • Confirm costs with suppliers, and add testing and end-of-life costs.
  • Ask the UV supplier for evidence of its dose, and specify an alarm and automatic shut-off (NSW Health, n.d.).
  • Check roofs and flashings for lead (Gardner & Vieritz, 2010) and the site for cultural heritage requirements.
  • Run a pilot slow-sand filter, and check the sizing against Port Stewart rainfall records.
  • Confirm who maintains the system and how batteries leave the community.

Next step: consult the Yintjingga Aboriginal Corporation and the Lama Lama community before any detailed design.

Appendix 1: Group charter

This charter records how Group 6 (Tutorial 1, Tanzeem) worked together on the EWB Challenge website. It was written up in October 2026 to describe the team’s actual way of working.

Purpose. The team worked together to design a shared rainwater system for Port Stewart and to present it clearly, with the Lama Lama community and the Yintjingga Aboriginal Corporation at the centre of the work.

Participation and workload. Every member took part and shared the workload. The team agreed who would take each section and divided the work fairly. The Week 10 presentation roles were Irene (background, current practices and existing solutions), Nusaibah (design solution and presentation design), Zaheen (problem description, user needs and how the design meets them), Zihao (criteria, prototype, implementation and costings) and Wenrui (solution components, other considerations and conclusion). Contributions to the website are listed in the Teamwork Declaration (Table 2).

Communication. The team worked in the weekly tutorial and online. A group chat was used for updates, questions, drafts and decisions. Members replied quickly, which kept the work moving between classes. The team did not hold separate in-person meetings.

Decision-making. Each member shared their own ideas before a decision was made. The team decided together once everyone had contributed, and agreed decisions were recorded in the group chat.

Standards. Members agreed to keep the work accurate, to cite sources, and to represent the Lama Lama people and community respectfully.

Appendix 2: Meeting minutes

The team did not hold separate formal meetings. Group work took place in the weekly tutorial and in the online group chat, where ideas, decisions and actions were recorded. Table 12 is a decision log compiled from that chat and from the tutorials.

Table 12. Decision log from the group chat and tutorials.
DateDecision or actionWho
Week 1Chose Design Opportunity 6.2, Drinking Water Quality and Treatment, for Port Stewart.Nusaibah
Weeks 4 to 5Agreed the four options to compare: repair the river filter, the 2020 bore intake, chemical treatment and cluster rainwater harvesting.All members
Week 5Chose cluster rainwater harvesting, with one system for each group of about five homes, as the design to develop.All members
Week 9Agreed the sections and speaking order for the Week 10 presentation.All members
Week 10Agreed to build the website on Google Sites, following the template.All members

Appendix 4: Statement of AI use

The team used generative AI. Two images, the prototype layout in Figure 10 and the system illustration in Figure 2, were AI-generated by the team using ChatGPT (OpenAI) and are labelled as such. The outlet label on Figure 2 was edited by the team. The location map in Figure 3 was drawn by the team using open coastline data.

The background research, design solution, costings and presentation content came from the team’s Week 10 work. The site guide is scripted and answers only from the website’s own content; it does not call a live AI service. AI output can be wrong, and the team is responsible for checking every claim and source.
